title: Advanced Integration Patterns (iPaaS, API Gateway, Event Mesh)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Advanced Integration Patterns (iPaaS, API Gateway, Event Mesh) ##### 78 integrations for 13 systems An enterprise integration audit found 78 point-to-point connections between 13 systems. Each had been built by a different team, at a different time, mapping one vendor's schema directly onto another's. The number that made the CTO wince was not 78. It was the theoretical maximum: with 13 systems, full point-to-point connectivity is *n(n−1)/2* = 78. They had built literally every possible connection. The consequence was that a field change in the CRM could require edits in up to twelve integrations, nobody knew which, and the only way to find out was to break things. Adding a fourteenth system would mean thirteen new integrations. The same 13 systems connected through a hub with a canonical model need **13 connections**. That is the structural argument for everything in this article, and Hohpe and Woolf's *Enterprise Integration Patterns* catalogue remains the shared vocabulary for it. ##### The core patterns Six patterns from the EIP catalogue account for most integration work: **Message router** — inspect a message and send it to the right destination. Your n8n Switch node and Make Router are implementations. **Message translator** — convert between formats and schemas. The transformation layer, and the pattern the canonical model organizes. **Content enricher** — augment a message with data fetched from elsewhere (add firmographics to a lead). **Content filter** — remove fields before forwarding, typically to strip PII or reduce payload size. **Aggregator** — combine multiple related messages into one (collect line items into an order). **Splitter** — break a composite message into parts (an order into individual fulfilment tasks). **Normalizer** — convert varied input formats into one common shape before processing. This is the pattern that makes the canonical model work. Recognizing these by name matters practically: when you can say "this is a splitter feeding an aggregator with a correlation ID," you stop reinventing solutions and start reusing known ones — including their known failure modes. ##### The canonical data model The fix for 78 integrations. Instead of mapping each system to every other, every system maps **to and from one internal schema**. ```text Point-to-point: n(n-1)/2 mappings 13 systems → 78 mappings Canonical: 2n mappings 13 systems → 26 mappings (13 in, 13 out) Adding system 14: +13 vs +2 ``` ```json { "$schema": "https://acme.internal/schemas/customer/v2.json", "type": "object", "required": ["customer_id", "email", "source", "source_updated_at"], "additionalProperties": false, "properties": { "customer_id": { "type": "string", "description": "Internal canonical ID" }, "email": { "type": "string", "format": "email" }, "full_name": { "type": ["string", "null"] }, "phone_e164": { "type": ["string", "null"], "pattern": "^\\+[1-9]\\d{6,14}$" }, "company": { "type": ["object", "null"], "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" }, "size_band": { "enum": ["1-10", "11-50", "51-200", "201-1000", "1000+"] } } }, "lifecycle_stage": { "enum": ["lead", "mql", "sql", "customer", "churned"] }, "source": { "type": "string" }, "source_record_id": { "type": "string" }, "source_updated_at": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" } } } ``` Design rules that make a canonical model succeed rather than become a fourth incompatible schema: - **Model your business domain**, not the union of every vendor's fields. If Salesforce and HubSpot disagree on lifecycle stage names, pick the one your business actually uses. - **Version it explicitly** (`/v2`) and treat it as a public contract — additive changes only within a version. - **Always carry provenance** (`source`, `source_record_id`, `source_updated_at`) so you can trace and reconcile. - **Use an anti-corruption layer** per system: one adapter that isolates that vendor's quirks so their weirdness never leaks into the canonical shape. The honest cost: canonical modelling is more work for the first two integrations and less for every one after. Below about four systems, point-to-point is genuinely fine. ##### Hub-and-spoke iPaaS The hub implements the canonical model and hosts the routing, translation and enrichment. Choosing the hub depends on scale and who maintains it: | | Zapier | Make | n8n | Workato / MuleSoft | |---|---|---|---|---| | Best for | Simple SaaS glue | Visual mid-complexity | Technical teams, self-hosted | Enterprise governance | | Canonical model support | Awkward | Workable | Good (sub-workflows) | First-class | | Governance / RBAC | Basic | Team features | Self-managed | Extensive | | Cost model | Per task | Per operation | Per execution / infra | Enterprise licence | For an automation engineer, **n8n as the hub** is usually the right answer: sub-workflows implement the map-in and map-out adapters, credentials are centralized, and cost does not scale with step count. The hub-and-spoke weakness is real and worth stating: **the hub is a single point of failure and a bottleneck**. Mitigate with queue-mode scaling, health checks, and — importantly — by not routing high-volume event traffic through it when a message bus would serve better. ##### API gateway The gateway sits at the network edge, in front of your services, and handles cross-cutting concerns so individual services do not each reimplement them. ```yaml # Kong declarative config services: - name: automation-api url: http://automation-api.internal:8000 routes: - name: webhooks paths: ["/v1/webhooks"] methods: [POST] plugins: - name: rate-limiting config: { minute: 600, policy: redis, redis_host: redis } - name: request-size-limiting config: { allowed_payload_size: 2 } # MB - name: correlation-id config: { header_name: X-Request-ID, generator: uuid, echo_downstream: true } - name: prometheus - name: partner-api url: http://automation-api.internal:8000 routes: - name: partner paths: ["/v1/partner"] plugins: - name: key-auth - name: rate-limiting config: { minute: 60, policy: redis } # tighter limit for partners - name: acl config: { allow: ["partners"] } ``` What the gateway earns you: **authentication and authorization in one place**, **per-consumer rate limiting** (the multi-tenant noisy-neighbour defence), **request validation and size limits**, **correlation ID injection** for tracing, **centralized metrics and logging**, and **routing and versioning** so you can shift traffic between service versions without client changes. The distinction that trips people up: an **API gateway** manages *inbound* traffic to your services; an **iPaaS hub** orchestrates *outbound* integration between systems. They are complementary layers, not alternatives. ##### Event mesh and pub/sub decoupling Hub-and-spoke still means the hub knows every consumer. An **event mesh** removes even that coupling: producers publish facts to a broker, and consumers subscribe to what interests them. ```text Hub-and-spoke: order service → hub → (hub knows: billing, warehouse, analytics) Event mesh: order service → "order.paid" topic ├→ billing subscribes ├→ warehouse subscribes └→ analytics subscribes (producer knows none of them) ``` The decisive advantage is **extensibility**: adding a fraud-check consumer requires zero changes upstream. The cost is traceability — the end-to-end process exists in no single place, which is why correlation IDs and distributed tracing become mandatory rather than nice-to-have. Event schemas need the same discipline as APIs. **CloudEvents** provides a standard envelope, and a schema registry with compatibility rules prevents a producer change from breaking every consumer simultaneously: ```json { "specversion": "1.0", "type": "com.acme.order.paid.v1", "source": "/services/checkout", "id": "evt_88213", "time": "2026-03-14T09:12:44Z", "subject": "ORD-1042", "datacontenttype": "application/json", "traceparent": "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01", "data": { "order_id": "ORD-1042", "total_minor": 499800, "currency": "INR" } } ``` The version in the `type` field is what lets `v1` and `v2` consumers coexist during a migration. ##### API versioning and contracts Three strategies: **URI path** (`/v1/orders`) — most visible and cache-friendly, the pragmatic default; **header-based** (`Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json`) — cleaner URLs, harder to test casually; and **query parameter** — simple but easy to forget. The rules that keep consumers working, regardless of strategy: - **Additive changes only** within a version: new optional fields, new endpoints. - **Never remove or rename a field**, or change its type or semantics. - **Never make an optional field required.** - **Deprecate with a timeline** — announce, add a `Deprecation` header, monitor which consumers still use it, then remove. - **Support N-1** for a defined window, typically 6–12 months. **Contract testing** enforces this automatically: the consumer publishes its expectations, the provider's CI verifies each build still satisfies them. That converts "we think this change is safe" into a failing build when it is not. ##### Strangler fig Named after the vine that grows around a tree and gradually replaces it — the pattern for migrating legacy integrations without a big-bang cutover. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph S1["Stage 1 — baseline"] A1[CRM] -->|direct P2P| B1[Billing] end subgraph S2["Stage 2 — facade + dual write"] A2[CRM] -->|direct P2P| B2[Billing] A2 -.new path.-> H2[Hub: canonical] -.shadow write.-> B2 H2 --> C2[(Compare
outputs)] end subgraph S3["Stage 3 — cut over, keep fallback"] A3[CRM] --> H3[Hub: canonical] --> B3[Billing] A3 -.dormant.-> B3 end subgraph S4["Stage 4 — remove legacy"] A4[CRM] --> H4[Hub: canonical] --> B4[Billing] end ``` The migration steps in practice: 1. **Introduce a facade.** New code calls the hub; the legacy path still runs. 2. **Dual-write and compare.** The hub writes to a shadow table while the legacy integration writes for real. Diff the outputs daily until they agree — this is where you discover the undocumented behaviours the legacy path had. 3. **Cut over incrementally.** Route 5% of traffic through the hub, then 25%, then 100%, with the legacy path ready to resume. 4. **Monitor, then decommission.** Only after a full cycle (including month-end, which surfaces edge cases nothing else does) do you delete the old integration. The discipline that makes this work: **never remove the old path until the new one has run correctly through a complete business cycle.** The temptation to delete early is strong and the cost of being wrong is an outage during month-end close. ##### Common pitfalls - **Point-to-point past four systems** — quadratic growth catches up quickly. - **A canonical model that is the union of all vendor fields**, which is just a fourth schema. - **No provenance fields**, making reconciliation impossible. - **Hub as a single point of failure** with no scaling or health checks. - **Routing high-volume event traffic through an iPaaS hub** where a broker belongs. - **Confusing gateway and iPaaS roles** — inbound versus outbound. - **Unversioned event schemas**, so one producer change breaks every consumer. - **Breaking API changes without deprecation**, silently breaking integrations you cannot see. - **Big-bang legacy migration** with no dual-write comparison period. - **Decommissioning before a full business cycle** has validated the new path. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **design a hub-and-spoke integration with a canonical data model** connecting CRM, billing and support through n8n and an API gateway — diagram plus config — and **plan a strangler-fig migration**. Do the arithmetic in your write-up: how many mappings the current design needs versus the canonical one, and what adding a fourth system costs under each. That number is the justification. The mini project is that design made concrete: the canonical JSON Schema with versioning and provenance, one map-in and one map-out sub-workflow per system, and a gateway config with per-consumer rate limits and correlation-ID injection. Build two systems fully; the third should then take a fraction of the time, which is the pattern proving itself. For the assignment, **apply the strangler-fig pattern on paper to migrate one legacy point-to-point integration to the hub without downtime**. Be specific about the dual-write comparison — what you compare, for how long, and what discrepancy rate you would accept before cutting over — and name the business cycle you would wait through before decommissioning. ##### Key takeaways - Point-to-point integration grows as n(n−1)/2; a canonical model with per-system adapters grows as 2n, and that difference decides maintainability. - Model the canonical schema on your business domain with explicit versioning and provenance, isolating vendor quirks in anti-corruption layers. - An API gateway centralizes inbound concerns (auth, rate limiting, correlation IDs); an iPaaS hub orchestrates outbound integration — use both. - Event meshes decouple producers from consumers entirely, at the cost of traceability, so version event schemas and propagate trace context. - Migrate legacy integrations with strangler fig: facade, dual-write and compare, incremental cutover, and decommission only after a full business cycle.
